# C# Fundamentals Section: Restructuring Plan

This document captures the decisions, rationale, and proposed outline for restructuring the C# Fundamentals section. It's the result of planning discussions informed by the [GitHub project board](https://github.com/orgs/dotnet/projects/225/views/1), the [C# standard](https://github.com/dotnet/csharpstandard), and
the [feature inclusion notes](feature-coverage.md#feature-coverage-decisions).

## Goals

1. **Fundamentals lives in a four-tier content structure.** The C# documentation follows a progressive organization: *Get started* for beginners new to programming or C#, *Fundamentals* for developers learning everyday C#, *Deep dives* (Focus/Advanced sections) for specialized or advanced topics, and *Reference* for complete language syntax and API details. Every article should include a tip near the top that identifies where the article sits in this progression and who it's written for. The tip should describe the types of readers who would benefit most, identify readers who might need to start with *Get started* content first (for example, developers new to programming, or developers unfamiliar with object-oriented concepts), and identify readers with relevant experience who can skip ahead (for example, experienced C# developers or other experienced developers in a similar language, like Java or C++, who can jump directly to *Deep dives* or *Reference*). Because Fundamentals readers don't yet carry C# vocabulary across articles, define every C# term at first use within the article — including terms the author considers obvious (for example, *dereference*, *type parameter* vs. *type argument*) — and link to the deeper reference. When a familiar term from another ecosystem helps orient the reader, use it once as a bridge to the C# term, then use the C# term consistently.
1. **Make Fundamentals complete.** A developer learning C# should be able to read the Fundamentals section and understand "Everyday C#" — the features and patterns used in the vast majority of production code. Fundamentals documents only *released* language features. Preview features (for example, C# 15 `closed` hierarchies) stay in the Language Reference until they ship; a feature isn't "everyday" before developers can use it in released code.
1. **Pull content toward the goal.** Rather than focusing on migrating content *out* of legacy sections (Tutorials, C# concepts, How-to, Programming guide), we focus on building a great Fundamentals section and pull content in as it fits.
1. **Teach through examples.** Most engineers learn software languages by reading and writing example code, not by reading *about* the language. Every article in the Fundamentals section should be example-heavy: short prose introduces a concept, then one or more code samples demonstrate it in context. Favor showing over telling. Keep each sample as small and focused as possible—demonstrate one concept per example. Don't introduce additional concepts, patterns, or API calls that aren't directly relevant to the point being made. If a reader has to understand something unrelated to follow the sample, the sample is doing too much. Samples must be readable on first pass: for any construct the sample isn't teaching, use the most familiar form (`while` or `foreach` before `for`; a regular method before a static factory). Add a brief intent comment on any line whose purpose isn't immediately obvious, including syntax a new C# developer might not recognize yet, such as spread elements in collection expressions. When the sample illustrates a decision, show *both* branches and include the result as a trailing comment (`// => …`) so readers correlate code to output without running it. When two syntaxes are equivalent, make the sample outputs identical so the equivalence is visible without extra explanation.
1. **Combine language foundations with practical design guidance.** The earlier two-part IA hypothesis proposed a [C# standard](https://github.com/dotnet/csharpstandard/blob/main/standard/README.md)-ordered sequence of compact syntax and semantics articles, followed by guidance on how to combine constructs. Bill has now approved **Building software** as the cross-cutting section: compare valid algorithmic approaches that can produce the same results but communicate different design intent to developers and coding agents. Its first four articles are authored and accepted in open PR [#56333](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/pull/56333), not merged. They live directly under `fundamentals/building-software/`, without the retired Functional techniques grouping. This resolves that section's label and initial placement, not the entire two-part hypothesis or the remaining OOP boundary. See [Decision 14](decisions.md#decision-14-building-software-purpose-and-initial-structure).
1. **Emphasize everday C#.** Everyday C# features get fuller explanations. Older features that readers (including AI agents and Copilots) already have extensive information about receive lighter treatment. All sample code uses the latest released syntax and idioms.
1. **Target audience.** Developers who know at least one other programming language and are learning C#, or C# developers updating their knowledge of the latest features and idioms. Not absolute beginners in programming.
1. **Samples showcase Everday C# feature sets.** All sample code across the Fundamentals section should incorporate the language features listed in [Include and explain](feature-coverage.md#include-and-explain), [Use in sample code without detailed explanation](feature-coverage.md#use-in-sample-code-without-detailed-explanation), and the relevant subsets from [Include a subset](feature-coverage.md#include-a-subset). This means even an article about, for example, exception handling should use collection expressions, file-scoped namespaces, nullable reference types, raw string literals, and other everyday C# features in its samples — not just the feature under discussion. Readers absorb these idioms organically by seeing them used consistently.
1. **Gently opinionated.** Guide new readers toward the recommended way to accomplish tasks in modern C#. When context supports a default, present it with a justification (for example, improved readability, better tooling support, stronger type safety, or reduced boilerplate). When valid alternatives communicate different designs, name the alternatives and explain the context and expectations each creates rather than prescribe a universal preference. Building software comparisons use short explanatory paragraphs and small examples, not unexplained rules. Section overviews introduce their long-term purpose, not the current PR's feature inventory. See [Decision 15](decisions.md#decision-15-durable-overviews-and-contextual-comparisons). Never describe older features as obsolete or deprecated, or suggest developers must update existing working code.
1. **Default to the current-project frame, and teach how to verify settings.** Most Fundamentals readers are either starting a new project or following along in a freshly created one, so the default frame for any setup or configuration statement is a current project from a recent template. That keeps the prose concrete and the samples runnable without setup detours. *Lead with the current-project assumption* — for example, "New projects from recent templates set `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` in the project file" — and don't open with hedges. *Immediately follow* such statements with a one- or two-sentence pointer that shows existing-project readers where to verify the setting in their own `.csproj` and how to enable it if it's missing. *Reserve full migration guidance for the migration articles*: when the existing-project path is more than a setting check (for example, planning a phased rollout), link out rather than inlining the strategy. When a feature is recommended as the fix for a diagnostic, run the code and confirm the diagnostic actually clears in the scenario being recommended.
1. **Apply a two-criteria fit test to every article and every section.** Every article — and every distinct *section* within an article being pulled into Fundamentals — must pass both filters before it lands in the section. *Filter A — universality:* the content is used by almost all C# developers almost all of the time. Niche scenarios, library-author concerns, large-codebase migration strategies, and runtime-internal details fail this filter. *Filter B — accessibility:* a developer with less than one month of .NET and C# experience can follow the content given the prerequisites already covered in Fundamentals. Apply the filters as follows. *When a section fails Filter A,* relocate the *text* — don't delete it — to the most appropriate existing home (Language Reference, a Deep dives section, or an Advanced section). Create a new file in that destination only when no clear home exists. *When an entire article fails Filter A,* leave it where it currently lives until that area is restructured; don't pull it into Fundamentals at all. The canonical illustration is the nullable-reference-type migration article: it targets existing large codebases that pre-date C# 8 and isn't fundamental, so the migration article stays in place — at `advanced-topics/update-applications/nullable-migration-strategies.md`, the "Update existing apps" area — and the Fundamentals NRT article only links out to it. Treat `advanced-topics/update-applications/` as the standing home for migration content that passes nowhere else: when a section's text addresses updating existing code rather than writing new code, relocate it there. *When content fails Filter B but passes Filter A,* rewrite rather than relocate: define vocabulary at first use, replace the example with one a beginner can read line-by-line, and lead with motivation. Failing Filter B is an editing problem, not a scoping problem.

## Include major topic types

The following table lists each topic type. Every section should include an *Overview*, any number of *Concepts* articles, pertinent *Tutorials*. Where necessary, *troubleshooting* and *how to* articles can be added. All *Reference* articles are in the *language reference section*.

**All content types should be example-heavy.** Short prose introduces or connects concepts; code samples do the teaching. Samples in every article should restrict features to the set of C# features in Goals 6 and 7, and [Decision 10](decisions.md#decision-10-example-heavy-articles-with-everyday-c-feature-saturation)).

Each content type has an associated `ms.topic` metadata value. Set this value in the article's YAML front matter so that audience engagement data can be tracked per content type. For more information, see the [ms.topic taxonomy](https://taxonomy.learn.microsoft.com/TaxonomyServiceAdminPage/#/taxonomy/detail/2022-03-24T09:00:00.4446095Z!adfc651d-18a3-4f76-9685-da59537f7431/ms.topic).

When creating or revising an article, first focus on making the content accurate, relevant, and example-heavy. Once the content is solid, apply the template for the article's content type to verify that the structure, required metadata, and sections align with the expected format.

For rule-heavy features — nullable analysis, raw string literals, pattern precedence, complexity claims, and similar — enumerate the rules as a structured list (a short lead sentence, then bullets or a labeled example) and verify each rule against the language spec or reference *before* review. Put Big-O and other complexity details in a `> [!TIP]` note rather than inline prose, and state them precisely. These features draw the most reviewer corrections when the rules are paraphrased loosely or stated from memory.

| Content type | `ms.topic` value | Template | What is it | When to use it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Overview | `overview` | [template-overview.md](../templates/template-overview.md) | An article explaining the feature from a technical point of view. And/or an article comparing features across related features. Leads with a motivating example before diving into details. | For new customers. To explain the feature or technology from a technical point of view. It isn't intended to define benefits or value prop; that would be in marketing content. |
| Tutorials | `tutorial` | [template-tutorial.md](../templates/template-tutorial.md) | Scenario-based procedures for top tasks using the feature. The focus is on showing the customer how to do the task, not on helping them set up their own environment. Code-first from the opening paragraph. | To show the single best procedure for completing a customer task. |
| Concepts | `concept` | [template-concept.md](../templates/template-concept.md) | In-depth explanation of functionality related to the feature that are fundamental to understanding and use. Each concept is illustrated with at least one focused code sample. | To explain what something is and define its critical functions, describe how something works, or provide guidelines for completing a task in varied situations. |
| How-to guides | `how-to` | [template-how-to-guide.md](../templates/template-how-to-guide.md) | Procedural articles that show the reader how to complete a task. Each step includes the code to accomplish it. | To provide the steps for completing a task. How-to guides differ from tutorials in that they can include optional information, explanations, and information to help inform decisions. |
| Troubleshooting articles | `troubleshooting` | [general-troubleshoot.md](../templates/general-troubleshoot.md) | Articles that help users solve a common issue. Include before-and-after code showing the problem and the fix. | To help resolve a specific error or problem that customers commonly run into, and would search on. |
| Reference | `reference` | *(no template)* | Documentation for language-based syntax and semantics. | To provide descriptions of things like settings, values, keywords, and configurations. These articles are where readers go to look up a specific value. |

> [!NOTE]
> F1 and helpviewer keywords belong only in the *Reference* section. Don't add them to Fundamentals articles (overviews, concepts, tutorials, how-to guides, or troubleshooting articles). Remove them if pulling content from other sources.

## Current reconciliation: Building software

As of 2026-10-16, Bill accepted the implementation and editorial task for
[#56333](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/pull/56333), **Start on building fundamentals sections**.
The PR remains **OPEN**, with `mergedAt=null`, at head
`4737e1c7fe82c91ed8e6d531a3a78a0f5e9cc11e` on `more-everyday-csharp`.
The articles, snippet projects, redirects, inbound links, and TOC changes described in
[TOC and articles](toc-and-articles.md#building-software) are authored in that PR, not shipped
or present as implementation on this planning branch. The latest commit reframes the overview
and lightly edits the three companion articles; it doesn't change snippets.

This reconciliation updates the five project-planning documents and the plan README, Phase F,
and verification/decisions log. It supersedes the retired Functional techniques grouping and
pending label/initial-placement questions. It doesn't complete the future combined-techniques
tutorial, approve a broader OOP reorganization, or audit unrelated phase delivery status.
